lines.text: אול 22 אול
the verb, but of wide extent in the
derivatives.
1. Pr. to roll, to twist, to twirl, as in
kindr. חוּל, חִיל, גִּיל, גָּלַל; comp. εἰλέω,
εἰλύω, ἴλλω, and see below under r. גָּלַל.—
Hence אַיִל a ram, from his twisted
horns; also אוּל belly.
2. Trop. to be strong, stout, powerful;
for the connection comp. in חוּל and חַיִל.
—Hence אֵל the Strong One, God; אֵלָה
terebinth, q. d. the strong tree; אַלּוֹן
an oak, Lat. robur; also אֱיָל, אֱיָלוּת,
strength, aid.
3. Trop. to be first, foremost, chief,
from the notion of strength and power;
so Arab. أَوَلَ to be foremost, to come out
first, أَوَّلُ first, primus, (pr. princeps, like
רִאשׁוֹן,) comp. Heb. יָאַל.—Hence אוּלִים
אֵילִים, the mighty, the chief, אוּלָם the
front part, q. v. אַיִל no. 2, and אֵילָם, a
projection on a building; אַוֶּלֶת no. 3, the
first place, rank.
אוּל m. 1. the belly, body, pr. a roll,
roller, from the round form; r. אוּל no. 1.
Ps. 73, 4. Arab. اأْلٌ, آلٌ.
2. Plur. the mighty, the powerful, the
chief. 2 K. 24, 15 Cheth. אוּלֵי הָאָרֶץ
the chief of the land. The Keri has the
more usual form אֵילֵי. R. אוּל no. 3.
I. אוּלַי compounded from אַי constr.
אוֹ, and לַי i. q. לַי, לֵא, לָא, not; comp.
אַחֲלֵי, לוּלֵי.
1. if not, unless, once Num. 22, 33
אוּלַי נָטְתָה מִפָּנַי וגו׳ unless she had turn-
ed from me, surely now I had slain thee.
Sept. εἰ μή. Aben Ezra well לוּלֵי.
2. whether not, Is. 47, 12; and hence
ellipt. [who knows] whether not, i. e. per-
haps, peradventure, expressing doubt,
fear, Gen. 24, 5. 27, 12. Josh. 9, 7; and
also hope, Gen. 16, 2. Am. 5, 15.—Hos.
8, 7 the stalk shall yield no meal, אוּלַי
יַעֲשֶׂה זָרִים יִבְלָעֻהוּ [or if] perhaps it
yield, strangers shall devour it. Jer. 21, 2.
—In like manner Arab. لَعَلَّ and عَلَّ
perhaps, is pr. whether not, ellipt. As to
its origin, for أَنْ, and its various forms
and use, see De Sacy Gramm. Arabe 1.
§ 867, and note. More nearly corre-
sponding are the Talmudic particles שֶׁמָּא
and דִּילְמָא pr. whether not, annon, then
whether perhaps, if perhaps, fortasse;
e. g. Pirke Aboth 2, 4 ‘ ne dicas: cum
otiosus fuero, discam, fortasse (שׁמא) non
eris otiosus.’ Berach 2, 1. 9. Also מאים
what if? perhaps, which is put for Heb.
אוּלַי Is. 47, 12.
II. אוּלַי pr. n. Ulai, Eulæus, a river
flowing by Susa in Persia, and emptying
itself into the united stream of the Eu-
phrates and Tigris, called by the Greeks
Choaspes, now Kerah. Dan. 8, 2. See
Hdot. 5. 49. Plin. H. N. 6. 27 or 31.
R. K. Porter’s Travels, Vol. II. p. 412,
and Map.
אוּלָם, אֻלָם, (Kamets impure,) Plur.
אֵלַמִּים, (r. אוּל no. 3,) pr. the anterior
part, front; hence
1. vestibule, porch, portico, 1 K. 7, 6
sq. Ez. 40, 7 sq. Spec. of the vestibule
or porch erected on the eastern front of
the temple of Solomon, Gr. ὁ πρόναος,
1 K. 6, 3. Joel 2, 17; more fully אוּלָם
יְהוָֹה 2 Chr. 15, 8. 29, 17. The altitude
of this porch is said (2 Chr. 3, 4) to have
been 120 cubits, while the height of the
temple itself was only 30 cubits, and its
length 60 cubits, 1 K. 6, 2. This would
give to the porch the form of a tower,
unless there is here an error in the text.
Perhaps for מאה ועשרים we may read
with Meyer and others אמות עשרים
twenty cubits.
2. Adv. pr. in front, and therefore op-
posite, on the contrary; hence trop. as a
strong adversative particle, but, but yet,
nay but, nevertheless, οὐ μὴν ἀλλά, as
Sept. well. Job 2, 5. 5, 8. 13, 3. Often
also וְאוּלָם, Sept. οὐ μὴν δὲ ἀλλά, Gen.
Where two adversative propositions
stand one after the other, the Hebrews
repeat the adversative particle, as in
Engl. e. g. אוּלָם—וְאוּלָם Job 13, 3. 4.
Comp. כִּי—וְכִי. Once in Job 17, 10
it is written אֻלָם, where some Mss.
falsely read אֻלָּם.—It may be worth
inquiry, whether this particle also, as
well as אוּלַי, may not be compounded
from אוּ i. q. אוֹ an, whether, and לָם i. q.
ܠܡܳܐ, لَمْ, not, in the ellipt. sense, [who
knows] whether not, i. q. but perhaps.
This conjecture would seem to be
supported by the Syriac word ܐܘܿܠܡܳܐ,

line_status.note: The last word carries two points: a patach under the ḥet and a ḥireq dot under the yod — it is חַיִל (ḥayil), not חִיל; the first word is plene חוּל with shureq.

Above the waw in line 1 only a single oblique stroke (fatha) is printed, no shadda — contrast line 2, where the waw clearly carries the w-shaped shadda plus fatha. So the printed form is أَوَلَ (Reading B), not أَوَّلَ.
Final word is printed plene אוּלִים (hireq under lamed, yod, final mem), not אוּלָם; Reading A is correct.

The letter after aleph is a full-height vav with a dot inside it (not a short yod as in A), but it also carries a segol beneath it and the lamed carries a plain segol with no dagesh (unlike B); the aleph has a patah. So neither reading matches: the printed word is אַוֶּלֶת.

Two alifs are printed before the lām (B's single-alif ألٌّ with shadda is wrong), but only the second alif carries a hamza/sukūn and the lām a tanwīn ḍamma; no fatḥa or hamza is printed on the first alif, so A over-points it. آلٌ matches both.
The word after "from" is printed aleph + patach + yod (אַי), not אוֹ; the אוֹ belongs to the start of line 2 ("constr. אוֹ, and לַי"). Reading B matches the print.
After "i. q." the three items are printed לַי (patach + yod), לֵא (tsere + aleph), לָא (qamets + aleph); the last has a qamets, not a holem, so Reading A's לֵי / לֹא sequence is wrong.
Printed left-to-right order is אַחֲלֵי first, then לוּלֵי; the lamed in אַחֲלֵי carries tsere (two dots), not patah. Reading A reverses the items and mis-points the lamed.
The print shows a visible space between the opening quote ‘ and "ne", and a thin space before the colon after "dicas" (period-typical French spacing); Reading B reproduces both, Reading A drops them.
The Hebrew is printed with a shin dot over the ש but no vowel points below and no dagesh in the mem — so A is wrong to omit the shin dot, and B is wrong to add segol, dagesh and qamets.
The Hebrew word מאים is printed unpointed (like שמא on the line above); there is no tsere under mem or hiriq under alef, so Reading B's vowels are invented.
Under the aleph of the second word the print shows three dots in a diagonal row (kibbutz), not two horizontal dots (tsere); אֻלָם is the expected defective counterpart of אוּלָם.

Under the initial aleph two dots sit side by side horizontally (tsere), not the three diagonal dots of qubbuts; this matches the tsere in אֵלָם on the preceding line. Rest of the line identical in both readings and matches the print.

Under the aleph the print shows three diagonal dots (qibbuts), not the two horizontal dots of tsere, and the lamed carries a dagesh dot inside it with qamets below — matching Reading B אֻלָּם, not A's אֵלָם.

The Syriac word is printed plene: after the initial alaph there is a clear waw (the round "o" form) carrying a dot above, then lamadh, mem with zqapha, final alaph. Reading A omits the waw entirely; Reading B matches the printed letters and points.
